newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK airport body rejects IATA's claims on charges.
newsitem.headline: HK airport body rejects IATA's claims on charges.

text.p: Hong Kong's Airport Authority (AA) on Tuesday rejected claims by the International Air Transport Association (IATA) that airport charge levels at the territory's future airport would harm Hong Kong's role as an aviation centre.

"Some of the recent figures quoted by IATA and others, such as an alleged loss of one million visitors a year to Hong Kong, are highly speculative," AA corporate development director Clinton Leeks told a news conference.

"As the level of fees has not yet been decided upon, such suggestions are alarmist rather than helpful to the common aim, which is to continue to develop Hong Kong's role as a centre of aviation in the region," he said.

Last month, the world airline body said the territory could lose a million passengers a year if moves to introduce high airline charges at its new Chek Lap Kok airport, scheduled to start operation next year, went ahead.
IATA also noted charges at the new airport in its first year of operation would represent a 146 percent increase over the estimated aeronautical charge at the existing Kai Tak airport.

"There is no point in comparing charges at Chek Lap Kok with those at Kai Tak, whose capacity is now saturated and whose facilities are ageing," said Leeks of the AA, an entity charged with developing and managing the new airport.
He said charges at the new airport would not be excessively higher than at Kai Tak.
"The new airport's charges will be fair and reasonable, and will represent good value for the services rendered," he said.

"In terms of levels...we are about in the middle of the range of the 20 or so airports that we have looked at," he said, adding those airports represented "a fair spread" from Asia, Europe and America.
Leeks said the IATA's remarks were based on the AA's business plan set in 1995, but some of the "key figures" in the plan had now changed in airlines' favour.
For instance, he said, the AA now estimated that the new airport needed to raise less than the originally forecast HK$4.7 billion in the first year of operation.
"Consultations with IATA and other groups over fees at the new airport at Chek Lap Kok are still in progress," he said.
The AA would hold talks with IATA on March 12 and 13, he said.
